# Gradient-Boosted Trees Are One INSTALL Away

Here is the whole setup. You need DuckDB 2.0.0 or newer, and then two lines:

```sql
INSTALL duckboost FROM community;
LOAD duckboost;
```

And here is the smallest train-and-predict loop I know how to write: fifty rows, one feature, and a perfectly linear target.

```sql
CREATE TABLE tiny AS
SELECT i::DOUBLE AS x, (2 * i + 1)::DOUBLE AS y FROM range(50) t(i);

CREATE TABLE tiny_model AS
SELECT duckboost_train(y, [x], MAP {'backend': 'native', 'n_estimators': '50', 'feature_names': 'x'}) AS model
FROM tiny;

SELECT x, y, round(duckboost_predict(model, [x]), 2) AS pred
FROM tiny_model, tiny
WHERE x IN (5, 25, 45)
ORDER BY x;
```

```text
┌────────┬────────┬────────┐
│   x    │   y    │  pred  │
│ double │ double │ double │
├────────┼────────┼────────┤
│    5.0 │   11.0 │  11.19 │
│   25.0 │   51.0 │   51.0 │
│   45.0 │   91.0 │  90.78 │
└────────┴────────┴────────┘
```

`duckboost_train()` is an aggregate, so it behaves like `sum()` or `avg()`: many rows in, one value out. That value is the model, stored as a JSON string. `duckboost_predict()` takes the string plus a list of features and returns a number.

Features always go in as a `DOUBLE[]` list, which is why you see `[x]` even with a single column. Everything else in this post is a variation on those two functions.

[`duckboost`](https://github.com/JavOrraca/duckboost){target="_blank"} is the DuckDB extension I maintain. It trains histogram gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT, the model family behind XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost) with a built-in trainer, evaluates them in SQL, and exports a trained model as a plain SQL query.

It reached the community extensions repository on October 23, 2026 through [community-extensions PR #3236](https://github.com/duckdb/community-extensions/pull/3236){target="_blank"}. The current release is [v0.0.4](https://github.com/JavOrraca/duckboost/releases/tag/v0.0.4){target="_blank"}, under an MIT license.

Thank you to the DuckDB team and the maintainers of [DuckDB community extensions](https://duckdb.org/community_extensions/){target="_blank"}. Their build pipeline compiles the extension for each platform, and that is the reason the install is one line.

# What DuckDB 2.0 Changes for This

DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS, codenamed "Cinnamon Teal", shipped on October 21, 2026. The [announcement](https://duckdb.org/2026/10/21/announcing-duckdb-200.html){target="_blank"} calls it the team's biggest feature release so far. The headline items are a polished Quack protocol with the new `CONNECT` statement, asynchronous I/O, a first-class `VARIANT` type, triggers, agent mode in the CLI, and a PEG-based SQL parser that is now the default.

None of those are what duckboost builds on. Three smaller facts from the announcement and the extension docs matter for this post:

- DuckDB 2.0 is an LTS release with support until at least October 2027, and duckboost v0.0.4 targets it. DuckDB 1.x clients cannot load the extension.
- The old single-arrow lambda syntax is disabled by default. The one lambda below uses the `lambda p:` form.
- DuckDB versions before 2.0 cannot read database files created by 2.0. The model store in this post is a `.duckdb` file, so read the [migration guide](https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/operations_manual/migration){target="_blank"} before you point an older client at it.

# Multivariate Regression in Plain SQL

Both examples use synthetic tables built with SQL, so nothing downloads and a render never touches the network. Instead of `random()`, I derive every column from `hash()` of the row number, which builds the same 3,000 rows however many threads DuckDB uses.^[The numbers below reproduced exactly across repeated runs on DuckDB 2.0.0. I would not promise that `hash()` output stays identical in future DuckDB versions, so read the metrics as "about this", not as a contract.]

The target is deliberately non-linear: a linear term, a sine of `x2`, a threshold on `x3` that switches on an `x4` effect, an `x1 * x2` interaction, and uniform noise. The noise has a standard deviation of about 0.82, so no model should be expected to land far below a holdout RMSE of 0.82.

For the split I use `duckboost_initial_split()`, a table macro that adds a `split` column holding `'train'` or `'test'`. It borrows the idea (not the code) of [rsample](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/){target="_blank"}'s `initial_split()`. The assignment is a hash of the row values plus the seed, so the same rows and seed give the same split.

```sql
-- 3,000 synthetic rows. hash() gives reproducible uniforms (no random() ordering surprises).
CREATE TABLE reg_data AS
WITH u AS (
  SELECT i AS id,
         (hash(i * 10 + 1) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS x1,
         (hash(i * 10 + 2) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS x2,
         (hash(i * 10 + 3) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS x3,
         (hash(i * 10 + 4) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS x4,
         (hash(i * 10 + 5) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS e1,
         (hash(i * 10 + 6) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS e2
  FROM range(3000) t(i)
)
SELECT id, x1, x2, x3, x4,
       (10 * x1 + 6 * sin(6 * x2) + 8 * (x3 > 0.5)::INT * x4 - 4 * x1 * x2
        + 2.0 * (e1 + e2 - 1))::DOUBLE AS y
FROM u;

-- 75/25 train/test split, reproducible with a seed
CREATE TABLE reg_split AS
FROM duckboost_initial_split('reg_data', prop := 0.75, seed := 42);

SELECT split, count(*) AS n, round(avg(y), 3) AS mean_y
FROM reg_split GROUP BY split ORDER BY split;
```

```text
┌─────────┬───────┬────────┐
│  split  │   n   │ mean_y │
│ varchar │ int64 │ double │
├─────────┼───────┼────────┤
│ test    │   750 │  5.948 │
│ train   │  2250 │  5.914 │
└─────────┴───────┴────────┘
```

That is 2,250 training rows and 750 test rows, with similar means on both sides. I like to see that before I train anything.

Now the model. Options travel in a `MAP` of strings, so numbers are quoted. Unknown keys raise an error instead of being ignored, so a typo in `'learning_rate'` fails loudly.

`'backend': 'native'` selects the built-in trainer. The docs describe it as dependency-free, single-threaded, and aimed at SQL-native workflows rather than replacing XGBoost, LightGBM, or CatBoost at every scale. That matches how I would use it.

```sql
-- Train on the training rows only
CREATE TABLE reg_models AS
SELECT duckboost_train(
  y, [x1, x2, x3, x4],
  MAP {
    'backend': 'native',
    'task': 'regression',
    'n_estimators': '200',
    'max_depth': '4',
    'learning_rate': '0.1',
    'min_samples_leaf': '5',
    'seed': '42',
    'feature_names': 'x1,x2,x3,x4'
  }
) AS model
FROM reg_split
WHERE split = 'train';
```

Predicting on the holdout is a cross join between the one-row model table and the test rows. Here are five predictions next to the truth:

```sql
-- Predict on the holdout
CREATE TABLE reg_preds AS
SELECT id, y, duckboost_predict(model, [x1, x2, x3, x4]) AS pred
FROM reg_models, reg_split
WHERE split = 'test';

SELECT id, round(y, 3) AS y, round(pred, 3) AS pred
FROM reg_preds ORDER BY id LIMIT 5;
```

```text
┌───────┬────────┬────────┐
│  id   │   y    │  pred  │
│ int64 │ double │ double │
├───────┼────────┼────────┤
│     3 │  6.356 │  5.236 │
│     8 │ 13.186 │ 14.225 │
│    17 │ 11.676 │  14.39 │
│    20 │  0.476 │  1.759 │
│    30 │  8.797 │  8.976 │
└───────┴────────┴────────┘
```

Metrics are ordinary SQL, which I prefer because I can group them by segment later. The baseline column is the RMSE you get by predicting the training mean for every test row.

```sql
-- Holdout metrics in plain SQL, next to a "predict the training mean" baseline
WITH train_mean AS (SELECT avg(y) AS m FROM reg_split WHERE split = 'train'),
     test_mean  AS (SELECT avg(y) AS ybar FROM reg_preds)
SELECT
  round(sqrt(avg((y - pred) ^ 2)), 3)                  AS rmse,
  round(avg(abs(y - pred)), 3)                         AS mae,
  round(1 - sum((y - pred) ^ 2) / sum((y - ybar) ^ 2), 3) AS r2,
  round(sqrt(avg((y - m) ^ 2)), 3)                     AS baseline_rmse
FROM reg_preds, train_mean, test_mean;
```

```text
┌────────┬────────┬────────┬───────────────┐
│  rmse  │  mae   │   r2   │ baseline_rmse │
│ double │ double │ double │    double     │
├────────┼────────┼────────┼───────────────┤
│  0.989 │  0.785 │  0.974 │         6.095 │
└────────┴────────┴────────┴───────────────┘
```

The model removes most of the error: RMSE falls from 6.095 to 0.989, which sits about 0.17 above the noise floor, and R2 is 0.974. The built-in evaluator should agree with the hand-written SQL, so I check:

```sql
-- Same numbers from duckboost's own evaluator
SELECT
  round(duckboost_evaluate_agg(model, y, [x1, x2, x3, x4], MAP {'metric': 'rmse'}), 3) AS rmse,
  round(duckboost_evaluate_agg(model, y, [x1, x2, x3, x4], MAP {'metric': 'mae'}), 3)  AS mae
FROM reg_models, reg_split
WHERE split = 'test';
```

```text
┌────────┬────────┐
│  rmse  │  mae   │
│ double │ double │
├────────┼────────┤
│  0.989 │  0.785 │
└────────┴────────┘
```

Same RMSE and MAE. The `metric` option also accepts `accuracy`, `logloss`, `brier_score`, and `roc_auc_ovr` for classification, which is where we go next.

# Multivariate Multi-Class Classification

Multi-class labels must be integer class indices from 0 to `n_classes - 1`, passed as `DOUBLE`. Map string labels with a `CASE` first. Set `'task': 'multiclass'` and duckboost fits one tree per class per boosting round, so 60 rounds on 3 classes is 180 trees.

The synthetic table has four features and three classes with a noisy, non-linear boundary. This time the split is stratified on `label`, so each class lands in train and test in the same proportions.

```sql
-- 3,000 synthetic rows, three classes (0, 1, 2) with a noisy, non-linear boundary
CREATE TABLE clf_data AS
WITH u AS (
  SELECT i AS id,
         (hash(i * 10 + 11) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS x1,
         (hash(i * 10 + 12) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS x2,
         (hash(i * 10 + 13) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS x3,
         (hash(i * 10 + 14) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS x4,
         (hash(i * 10 + 15) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS e1,
         (hash(i * 10 + 16) % 1000000) / 1000000.0 AS e2
  FROM range(3000) t(i)
),
s AS (
  SELECT *,
         3 * x1 + 2 * sin(5 * x2) + 0.6 * (e1 - 0.5) AS score_a,
         4 * x3 * x4 + 0.6 * (e2 - 0.5)              AS score_b
  FROM u
)
SELECT id, x1, x2, x3, x4,
       CASE WHEN score_a < 1.6 THEN 0
            WHEN score_b > 1.2 THEN 2
            ELSE 1 END::DOUBLE AS label
FROM s;

SELECT label::INT AS label, count(*) AS n FROM clf_data GROUP BY label ORDER BY label;

CREATE TABLE clf_split AS
FROM duckboost_initial_split('clf_data', prop := 0.75, strata := label, seed := 42);
```

```text
┌───────┬───────┐
│ label │   n   │
│ int32 │ int64 │
├───────┼───────┤
│     0 │  1290 │
│     1 │  1135 │
│     2 │   575 │
└───────┴───────┘
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE clf_models AS
SELECT duckboost_train(
  label, [x1, x2, x3, x4],
  MAP {
    'backend': 'native',
    'task': 'multiclass',
    'n_estimators': '60',
    'max_depth': '3',
    'learning_rate': '0.15',
    'min_samples_leaf': '5',
    'seed': '42',
    'feature_names': 'x1,x2,x3,x4'
  }
) AS model
FROM clf_split
WHERE split = 'train';
```

`duckboost_predict()` returns the most likely class index. `duckboost_predict_proba()` returns a list with one softmax probability per class. SQL lists are 1-based, so class `k` sits at position `k + 1`, which matters in the log loss below.

```sql
CREATE TABLE clf_preds AS
SELECT id, label,
       duckboost_predict(model, [x1, x2, x3, x4])       AS pred_class,
       duckboost_predict_proba(model, [x1, x2, x3, x4]) AS proba
FROM clf_models, clf_split
WHERE split = 'test';

SELECT id, label::INT AS label, pred_class::INT AS pred_class,
       list_transform(proba, lambda p: round(p, 3)) AS proba
FROM clf_preds ORDER BY id LIMIT 5;
```

```text
┌───────┬───────┬────────────┬───────────────────────┐
│  id   │ label │ pred_class │         proba         │
│ int64 │ int32 │   int32    │       double[]        │
├───────┼───────┼────────────┼───────────────────────┤
│     2 │     1 │          1 │ [0.231, 0.767, 0.002] │
│     3 │     0 │          0 │ [0.999, 0.001, 0.0]   │
│     4 │     2 │          2 │ [0.116, 0.088, 0.796] │
│     8 │     2 │          2 │ [0.004, 0.052, 0.944] │
│    10 │     0 │          0 │ [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]       │
└───────┴───────┴────────────┴───────────────────────┘
```

Now the holdout metrics. Accuracy and log loss are one query. The majority-class accuracy is the floor to beat, meaning what you get by always predicting the most common training class.

```sql
SELECT round(avg((pred_class = label)::INT), 4) AS accuracy,
       round(-avg(ln(greatest(proba[(label + 1)::INT], 1e-15))), 4) AS log_loss
FROM clf_preds;

-- Baseline: always predict the most common training class
SELECT round(avg((label = (SELECT mode(label) FROM clf_split WHERE split = 'train'))::INT), 4)
         AS majority_class_accuracy
FROM clf_preds;
```

```text
┌──────────┬──────────┐
│ accuracy │ log_loss │
│  double  │  double  │
├──────────┼──────────┤
│    0.944 │   0.1452 │
└──────────┴──────────┘
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ majority_class_accuracy │
│         double          │
├─────────────────────────┤
│                  0.4293 │
└─────────────────────────┘
```

Accuracy is 0.944 against a 0.4293 floor, and log loss is 0.1452. A confusion matrix is one `PIVOT` away, with true classes in rows and predicted classes in columns:

```sql
-- Confusion matrix: rows are the true class, columns are the predicted class
PIVOT (SELECT label::INT AS actual, pred_class::INT AS predicted FROM clf_preds)
ON predicted USING count(*) GROUP BY actual ORDER BY actual;
```

```text
┌────────┬───────┬───────┬───────┐
│ actual │   0   │   1   │   2   │
│ int32  │ int64 │ int64 │ int64 │
├────────┼───────┼───────┼───────┤
│      0 │   308 │    11 │     3 │
│      1 │     9 │   268 │     7 │
│      2 │     3 │     9 │   132 │
└────────┴───────┴───────┴───────┘
```

Most mistakes are between neighboring classes, 11 true zeros predicted as ones and 9 true ones predicted as zeros, which is what I expect from a boundary I blurred with noise. The built-in evaluator reports the same accuracy and log loss, plus a one-vs-rest AUC:

```sql
-- duckboost's own evaluator on the same holdout
SELECT
  round(duckboost_evaluate_agg(model, label, [x1, x2, x3, x4], MAP {'metric': 'accuracy'}), 4) AS accuracy,
  round(duckboost_evaluate_agg(model, label, [x1, x2, x3, x4], MAP {'metric': 'logloss'}), 4)  AS log_loss,
  round(duckboost_evaluate_agg(model, label, [x1, x2, x3, x4], MAP {'metric': 'roc_auc_ovr'}), 4) AS auc_ovr
FROM clf_models, clf_split
WHERE split = 'test';
```

```text
┌──────────┬──────────┬─────────┐
│ accuracy │ log_loss │ auc_ovr │
│  double  │  double  │ double  │
├──────────┼──────────┼─────────┤
│    0.944 │   0.1452 │  0.9931 │
└──────────┴──────────┴─────────┘
```

# Saving the Model: As an Object and as SQL

A duckboost model is a `VARCHAR` containing JSON. The docs call it an opaque document, so a table is a perfectly good model store. I keep the name next to the model, and in a real project I would add a version, a training date, and the holdout metrics as columns too.

```sql
-- 1) The model object is a VARCHAR holding JSON, so a table is a model store
CREATE TABLE saved_models AS
SELECT 'reg_gbdt_v1' AS model_name, now() AS saved_at, model FROM reg_models
UNION ALL
SELECT 'clf_gbdt_v1', now(), model FROM clf_models;

SELECT model_name, length(model) AS json_chars, left(model, 60) AS model_prefix
FROM saved_models ORDER BY model_name;
```

```text
┌─────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ model_name  │ json_chars │                         model_prefix                         │
│   varchar   │   int64    │                           varchar                            │
├─────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ clf_gbdt_v1 │     328571 │ {"duckboost_version":1,"backend":"reference","task":"multicl │
│ reg_gbdt_v1 │     632561 │ {"duckboost_version":1,"backend":"reference","task":"regress │
└─────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Because that table lives in a database file, a new process can reuse the model. I quit the shell, reopened `duckdb duckboost_demo.duckdb`, and scored the test rows again with the stored regression model:

```sql
-- New process, new connection. Load duckboost and reuse the stored model object.
LOAD duckboost;

CREATE TABLE reg_preds_reloaded AS
SELECT s.id, duckboost_predict(m.model, [s.x1, s.x2, s.x3, s.x4]) AS pred
FROM saved_models m, reg_split s
WHERE m.model_name = 'reg_gbdt_v1' AND s.split = 'test';

SELECT count(*) AS n_rows,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.pred = b.pred) AS identical_rows,
       max(abs(a.pred - b.pred)) AS max_abs_diff
FROM reg_preds a JOIN reg_preds_reloaded b USING (id);
```

```text
┌────────┬────────────────┬──────────────┐
│ n_rows │ identical_rows │ max_abs_diff │
│ int64  │     int64      │    double    │
├────────┼────────────────┼──────────────┤
│    750 │            750 │          0.0 │
└────────┴────────────────┴──────────────┘
```

All 750 predictions are identical to the ones from before the restart. The extension is still needed for this path, because `duckboost_predict()` does the scoring.

The second form needs no extension at all. `duckboost_to_sql()` takes the model, a table name, and the feature column names, and returns a `SELECT` that scores that table. `separate_trees` computes one column per tree and sums them, `keep_columns` carries your ID column through, and `proba` adds one `proba_k` column per class for classifiers.

Here I write each query to a file. Casting to `BLOB` and using `FORMAT blob` writes the text untouched, with no CSV quoting in the way:

```sql
-- 2) Export to plain SQL. Views name the holdout rows so the SQL has a table to score.
CREATE VIEW reg_test AS SELECT id, x1, x2, x3, x4 FROM reg_split WHERE split = 'test';
CREATE VIEW clf_test AS SELECT id, x1, x2, x3, x4 FROM clf_split WHERE split = 'test';

COPY (
  SELECT duckboost_to_sql(
    model, 'reg_test', ['x1', 'x2', 'x3', 'x4'],
    MAP {'separate_trees': 'true', 'prediction_alias': 'pred', 'keep_columns': 'id'}
  )::BLOB
  FROM saved_models WHERE model_name = 'reg_gbdt_v1'
) TO 'reg_model.sql' (FORMAT blob);

COPY (
  SELECT duckboost_to_sql(
    model, 'clf_test', ['x1', 'x2', 'x3', 'x4'],
    MAP {'separate_trees': 'true', 'prediction_alias': 'pred_class', 'keep_columns': 'id', 'proba': 'true'}
  )::BLOB
  FROM saved_models WHERE model_name = 'clf_gbdt_v1'
) TO 'clf_model.sql' (FORMAT blob);
```

The regression export is 878,484 bytes of SQL text and the classifier export is 298,045 bytes. That is a lot to read and no trouble to ship.

Now the part that matters. In a fresh process, without loading duckboost, I ran the exported text and compared it with the predictions `duckboost_predict()` made earlier. Attempt 1 runs the text as-is:

```sql
-- New process, duckboost is NOT loaded. Only DuckDB's built-in SQL runs from here.
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE extension_name = 'duckboost' AND loaded) AS duckboost_loaded
FROM duckdb_extensions();

-- Attempt 1: run the exported text as-is
SET VARIABLE reg_sql_raw = (SELECT content FROM read_text('reg_model.sql'));
SELECT count(*), max(pred) FROM query(getvariable('reg_sql_raw'));
```

```text
┌──────────────────┐
│ duckboost_loaded │
│      int64       │
├──────────────────┤
│                0 │
└──────────────────┘
Conversion Error: Casting value "13.06043230907708435666831746849372420" to type DECIMAL(38,37) failed: value is out of range!
```

The first line confirms the extension is not loaded. The second is the failure, which I explain in the callout below. The fix is a small macro that rewrites the text before DuckDB parses it, and then the comparison queries run:

```sql
-- Attempt 2: write the 17-digit literals as DOUBLEs (append e0), then run
CREATE MACRO as_doubles(sql) AS
  regexp_replace(sql, '([0-9]+\.[0-9]+)([^0-9e.])', '\1e0\2', 'g');

SET VARIABLE reg_sql = (SELECT as_doubles(content) FROM read_text('reg_model.sql'));
SET VARIABLE clf_sql = (SELECT as_doubles(content) FROM read_text('clf_model.sql'));

CREATE TABLE reg_preds_sql AS FROM query(getvariable('reg_sql'));
CREATE TABLE clf_preds_sql AS FROM query(getvariable('clf_sql'));

-- Regression: exported SQL vs. the predictions duckboost_predict made earlier
SELECT count(*) AS n_rows,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.pred = b.pred) AS identical_rows,
       max(abs(a.pred - b.pred)) AS max_abs_diff
FROM reg_preds a JOIN reg_preds_sql b USING (id);

-- Classification: what the exported query returns
SELECT column_name, column_type FROM (DESCRIBE clf_preds_sql);

SELECT count(*) AS n_rows,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.pred_class = b.pred_class) AS same_class,
       max(greatest(abs(a.proba[1] - b.proba_0),
                    abs(a.proba[2] - b.proba_1),
                    abs(a.proba[3] - b.proba_2))) AS max_abs_proba_diff
FROM clf_preds a JOIN clf_preds_sql b USING (id);
```

```text
┌────────┬────────────────┬──────────────┐
│ n_rows │ identical_rows │ max_abs_diff │
│ int64  │     int64      │    double    │
├────────┼────────────────┼──────────────┤
│    750 │            750 │          0.0 │
└────────┴────────────────┴──────────────┘
┌─────────────┬─────────────┐
│ column_name │ column_type │
│   varchar   │   varchar   │
├─────────────┼─────────────┤
│ id          │ BIGINT      │
│ pred_class  │ INTEGER     │
│ proba_0     │ DOUBLE      │
│ proba_1     │ DOUBLE      │
│ proba_2     │ DOUBLE      │
└─────────────┴─────────────┘
┌────────┬────────────┬────────────────────┐
│ n_rows │ same_class │ max_abs_proba_diff │
│ int64  │   int64    │       double       │
├────────┼────────────┼────────────────────┤
│    750 │        750 │                0.0 │
└────────┴────────────┴────────────────────┘
```

With the rewrite, the exported regression SQL matched all 750 predictions exactly, and the classifier SQL matched all 750 classes and every probability to a maximum difference of 0.0.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The DECIMAL gotcha in v0.0.4
Attempt 1 failed. The exported query writes leaf values and the learning rate as 17-digit literals such as `0.10000000000000001`, and DuckDB reads a literal like that as a `DECIMAL`. Summing hundreds of them can overflow, which is the error above.

The `as_doubles()` macro appends `e0` to every decimal literal so DuckDB treats it as a `DOUBLE`, the same arithmetic `duckboost_predict()` uses. Smaller ensembles sometimes ran without the rewrite in my tests and came back as a `DECIMAL` column, so whether it fails depends on the model.

I apply the rewrite every time. If you are on a later duckboost release, try attempt 1 first, since the rewrite may no longer be needed.
:::

# Importing XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost Dumps

If you already train with [XGBoost](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost){target="_blank"}, [LightGBM](https://github.com/microsoft/LightGBM){target="_blank"}, or [CatBoost](https://github.com/catboost/catboost){target="_blank"}, `duckboost_import()` converts a model dump into the same JSON model. After that, `duckboost_predict()`, `duckboost_predict_proba()`, and `duckboost_to_sql()` all work on it.

The docs list the inputs it reads: XGBoost JSON from `dump_model(..., dump_format='json')`, LightGBM text from `booster_.save_model()`, and CatBoost JSON from `save_model(..., format='json')`. In the community build CatBoost is import-only, and unsupported LightGBM objectives such as `poisson` are rejected rather than skipped.

```sql
-- Shape of the call; swap in your own dump file
SELECT duckboost_import(
  'lightgbm',
  (SELECT content FROM read_text('lgb_model.txt'))
) AS model;
```

I ran this form against the tiny fixture dumps in the repo's test folder, not against a production model, so treat that as a smoke test. The [import vignette](https://javorraca.github.io/duckboost/vignettes/import-dumps.html){target="_blank"} has the details for each format, including how learning rate and missing values are handled.

# Calling It from R

I live in R most days, and the extension works through the `duckdb` R package as long as the engine is 2.0.0 or newer. I ran this with the CRAN `duckdb` 2.0.0 package and DBI, using the same fifty-row loop as the top of the post:

```r
library(DBI)

con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
invisible(dbExecute(con, "INSTALL duckboost FROM community"))
invisible(dbExecute(con, "LOAD duckboost"))

invisible(dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE tiny AS
  SELECT i::DOUBLE AS x, (2 * i + 1)::DOUBLE AS y FROM range(50) t(i)
"))

invisible(dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE tiny_model AS
  SELECT duckboost_train(
    y, [x],
    MAP {'backend': 'native', 'n_estimators': '50', 'feature_names': 'x'}
  ) AS model
  FROM tiny
"))

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT x, y, round(duckboost_predict(model, [x]), 2) AS pred
  FROM tiny_model, tiny
  WHERE x IN (5, 25, 45)
  ORDER BY x
")

dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

```text
   x  y  pred
1  5 11 11.19
2 25 51 51.00
3 45 91 90.78
```

# Where I Would Use It

I reach for duckboost when the data already lives in DuckDB, the table is moderate in size, and the model has to travel as SQL. That last part is the point: a scoring query with no Python runtime and no extension is easy to review and easy to run in a place where you cannot install anything.

I would not reach for it for very large training sets. The docs are direct about the limits: training is single-threaded, all training rows are materialized in memory, and there are no monotonic constraints. The README also labels the project experimental, and v0.0.4 is early, so pin your versions.

For anything bigger, train with XGBoost, LightGBM, or CatBoost, then import the dump. The inspiration for the SQL export is Posit's [orbital](https://posit-dev.github.io/orbital/){target="_blank"}, which converts trained scikit-learn and tidymodels pipelines into SQL, and I wanted a similar loop inside DuckDB.
